content: Pus is a whitish-yellow or yellow substance that forms as part of the body’s inflammatory response to infection, particularly in areas affected by pyogenic bacterial infections. When pus accumulates in an enclosed tissue space, it is referred to as an abscess. If it collects visibly within or beneath the epidermis, it is termed a pustule or pimple. Pus is composed of both dead and living white blood cells that migrate into the intercellular spaces surrounding the affected cells. Substances or conditions that lead to the formation of pus are described as suppurative, pyogenic, or purulent. If both mucus and pus are produced, the condition is referred to as mucopurulent. The composition of pus includes a thin, protein-rich fluid known as liquor puris and dead neutrophils, which are a type of white blood cell involved in the body’s innate immune response. Neutrophils are produced in the bone marrow and released into the bloodstream. When an infection occurs, neutrophils are directed to the site of infection through a process called chemotaxis, which is typically triggered by cytokines released by macrophages that detect invading pathogens. At the site of infection, neutrophils engulf and destroy bacteria. After performing their function, the neutrophils die and are subsequently phagocytosed by macrophages, which further break them down. The resulting viscous material, composed of these dead neutrophils, is what we recognize as pus. Neutrophils are the most abundant type of leukocyte (white blood cell) in human blood, accounting for approximately 40% to 75% of all leukocytes. The presence of pus in a wound or on dry skin is a clear indication of infection and necessitates cleaning with an antiseptic to prevent further complications. While pus is typically whitish-yellow in color, its appearance can vary under certain conditions. For example, blue pus may be observed in infections caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa due to the production of a bacterial pigment called pyocyanin. Amoebic abscesses in the liver can produce brownish pus, while pus mixed with blood may take on a reddish tint. Additionally, pus can sometimes emit a noticeable odor, which may vary depending on the underlying infection.
